I Scanned a Jenkins AMI Without Launching It. Inspector Found 226 Vulnerabilities.

Now you can find software and package vulnerabilities in your AMIs without launching an EC2 instance.

Inspector already scanned EC2, Lambda and ECR. AMIs were the blind spot: you couldn’t see what was vulnerable in one until you launched it. I tried the new AMI scanning on a Jenkins image, ran into two default settings that kept it out of coverage, and got 226 findings from an image that had never run.

// 01

What Amazon Inspector already did

Most of us know Amazon Inspector as the service that scans EC2 instances and flags what’s wrong with them. It looks at the packages installed on an instance and matches them against known vulnerabilities, either through the SSM Agent or agentless through EBS snapshots.

It does more than that, though. Before this release, Inspector already covered:

What it scansWhat it tells you
EC2 instancesVulnerable OS and application packages on running instances.
Network reachabilityWhich ports on an instance are open to the internet, and the path that makes them reachable: security group, NACL, internet gateway.
Lambda functionsVulnerable dependencies in your function packages, and with code scanning, problems in the code itself.
ECR imagesVulnerable packages in container images, on push and continuously after that.

There was one thing it couldn’t look at: the AMI itself.

// 02

The gap: AMIs sitting on the shelf

The last year has been rough for vulnerabilities. Critical CVEs keep landing, and some get exploited within hours of disclosure. React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182) is a good example: a CVSS 10.0 remote code execution bug in React Server Components, with exploitation attempts showing up within hours of it going public. Every time something like that drops, the question is the same: where are we running the vulnerable version?

For running instances, Inspector already answers that. For AMIs, it couldn’t. Golden images, Jenkins images, old base images kept “just in case” all sit in the account, and nobody knows what’s inside them until someone launches an instance from one. By then, the vulnerable packages are already running.

The workaround was to launch a temporary instance, let Inspector scan it, read the findings and terminate it. AWS even published a Step Functions pattern for this. It worked, but it was a lot of moving parts just to ask “is this image safe?”

// 03

What changed on November 2

On November 2, AWS extended Amazon Inspector to scan EC2 AMIs directly. No instance launch and no agent. Inspector reads the image and reports the software and package vulnerabilities in it, so you can fix the image before anyone launches from it.

You get two ways to scan:

  • On-demand: scan one AMI from the EC2 console or CLI. Results show up on the AMI itself.
  • Continuous: Inspector watches the AMIs that match your rules and rescans them when new CVEs come out. Results show up in the Inspector console.

The part I like most is the control over which AMIs get scanned. Most accounts have plenty of AMIs nobody cares about, and you don’t want to pay to scan them or wade through their findings.

SettingOptionsWhy you’d use it
Scan modeExclusion-based or inclusion-basedScan everything except tagged AMIs, or scan only AMIs with a tag you choose.
AWS Backup and DLM imagesExclude or includeBackup and lifecycle images are copies of what’s already running and already scanned.
Copied imagesExclude or includeAMIs copied from another region. Exclude them if the source is scanned, include them if the copy is what you launch from.
Created withinNumber of daysOnly scan recently built AMIs.
Last launched withinNumber of daysOnly scan AMIs people are actually using.

An AMI qualifies for continuous scanning if it matches either date rule and isn’t excluded. Here’s the full decision path:

This is the kind of control that makes a security feature usable. You decide which images matter, and Inspector keeps watching those.

// 04

Security terms you’ll see in the findings

If you’re new to security, the findings page throws a lot of acronyms at you. These are the ones that show up in this post.

CVE

A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) ID is a public identifier for one known vulnerability, like CVE-2026-42523. The ID is just a name. It tells you nothing about how bad the bug is. Everyone, from AWS to your Linux vendor, uses the same ID, which is what lets Inspector match a package version to a known problem.

CVSS

CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) is the score that says how severe a CVE is, from 0 to 10. The score maps to the severity labels you see everywhere:

CVSS scoreSeverity
0.0None
0.1 to 3.9Low
4.0 to 6.9Medium
7.0 to 8.9High
9.0 to 10.0Critical

The score comes from a vector, a short string that describes the attack. Here’s the start of the one for the Critical finding later in this post:

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/...
PartMeaning
AV:NAttack vector: network. It can be attacked remotely.
AC:LAttack complexity: low. No special conditions needed.
PR:LPrivileges required: low. The attacker needs a basic account.
UI:RUser interaction: required. A victim has to do something, like open a page.
S:CScope: changed. The impact reaches beyond the vulnerable component.

Reading the vector tells you more than the number does. A 9.0 that needs a logged-in user is a different problem from a 9.0 that anyone on the internet can hit.

EPSS

EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) estimates the probability that a CVE will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days, from 0 to 1. CVSS says how bad it would be. EPSS says how likely it is to happen. An EPSS of 0.00281 means about a 0.28% chance.

CWE

A CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) is the type of mistake behind the bug. CWE-79 is cross-site scripting, CWE-502 is unsafe deserialization. Many CVEs share one CWE.

GHSA and related vulnerabilities

The same bug often has more than one ID. A GHSA-… ID is a GitHub Security Advisory, common for open-source packages. Inspector lists these under related vulnerabilities.

Fix available and exploit available

Two columns in Inspector that matter a lot for prioritising. Fix available means a patched version exists, so you can actually do something today. Exploit available means public exploit code exists, so someone else can too.

Vulnerability database search

Inspector has a built-in lookup for all of this. In the Inspector console, open Vulnerability database search, paste a CVE ID, and you get the description, CVSS, EPSS, CWE, and any vendor or CISA notes on one page. I use it later in this post for the Critical finding.

// 05

Trying it: an on-demand scan from EC2

I tested this on a private AMI called Jenkins. Two details about it end up mattering:

  • It was copied from us-east-1. The description says [Copied ami-03ca21734ca0e44d9 from us-east-1] Jenkins.
  • It was created on 23 October 2026 and never launched.

Open the AMI in the EC2 console, choose Actions, and under Security pick Scan for vulnerabilities.

EC2 confirms the scan has started and points you to the AMI’s Security tab.

While the scan runs, every count on the Security tab is zero. That means it isn’t finished, not that the image is clean.

On-demand results stay on the AMI’s Security tab in EC2 and in the CLI. They don’t appear in the Inspector console. Keep that in mind, because Inspector was about to tell me something very different about the same AMI.

// 06

Turning on continuous scanning

For ongoing coverage, activate Inspector. In an AWS Organizations setup, the activation page also offers to delegate administration to another account, and Inspector updates the delegation policy so that account can manage Inspector policies.

I activated just this account. Machine image scanning is its own scan type, next to EC2, ECR and Lambda.

The settings live under Scan settings → Machine images. My defaults were exclusion-based, copied images excluded, Backup and DLM images excluded, and both date rules at 14 days.

Compare that with my AMI: copied from another region, created more than 14 days ago, never launched. It fails both date rules and matches an exclusion. Here’s how its status changed as I fixed each one:

  1. Scan eligibility expired

    With the defaults. Outside both 14-day windows.

  2. Excluded by tag

    After widening both windows to 60 days. Still a copied image.

  3. Pending initial scan

    After including copied images.

// 07

Problem 1: Scan eligibility expired

Resource coverage showed my AMI under Not scanning.

The AMI page in Inspector shows why: created on October 23, never launched. Both 14-day rules fail.

Golden images often sit for weeks between launches, so 14 days is short for them. I set both rules to 60 days.

// 08

Problem 2: Excluded, with no exclusion tag

After saving, the status changed to Excluded by tag.

I never set an exclusion tag. The cause was the copied-images setting:

My AMI is a copy from us-east-1, so it was filtered out, and the console reported it as Excluded by tag. If you see that status with no tag set, check this box.

I unticked Exclude copied machine images and kept the Backup and DLM exclusion.

The status moved to Pending initial scan.

// 09

What the on-demand scan found

Meanwhile, the on-demand scan finished.

226 findings in an AMI that had never been launched: 1 Critical, 40 High, 118 Medium and 67 Low. 225 of them have a fix available, so this is an image that hasn’t been updated, not one with unfixable problems.

The Scan history keeps one row per on-demand run. Mine took 6 minutes 43 seconds.

The top findings by score:

  • CVE-2026-42523, Critical, 9: the Jenkins GitHub plugin.
  • CVE-2026-57281, High, 8.5: the Jenkins Script Security plugin.
  • CVE-2026-93320, High, 8.2: docker.

The top two are Jenkins plugins, which are Java packages bundled with the application, not OS packages. Inspector found them inside the image’s file system. Click File paths to see where:

/var/lib/jenkins/plugins/github-pullrequest/META-INF/maven/org.jenkins-ci.plugins/github-pullrequest/pom.xml
/var/lib/jenkins/plugins/github-branch-source/META-INF/maven/org.jenkins-ci.plugins/github-branch-source/pom.xml

The flagged component is the GitHub plugin, but the paths point into two other plugins, github-pullrequest and github-branch-source. It looks like both reference the vulnerable version, so updating one plugin probably isn’t enough. Check both, rebuild and rescan.

// 10

Looking up the Critical CVE

This is where the vulnerability database search earns its place. I searched for CVE-2026-42523:

FieldValue
AffectedJenkins GitHub Plugin 1.46.0 and earlier
CWECWE-79, stored cross-site scripting
CVSS v3 (NVD)9, Critical
Who can exploit itLogged-in users with Overall/Read permission
EPSS0.00281, about 0.28%
CISA remediation actionNone listed

In plain terms, the plugin puts the job URL into JavaScript without handling it safely. A logged-in user with read access can store a script that runs in someone else’s browser, including an admin’s.

This is where the terms from earlier help. CVSS says Critical. The vector says the attacker needs an account (PR:L) and a victim has to open a page (UI:R). EPSS says exploitation is unlikely in the next month. On a Jenkins server with a few trusted users, that lowers the urgency. On one where lots of people have read access, it doesn’t. The fix is a plugin upgrade past 1.46.0, so I’d do it either way.

// 11

The continuous scan in Inspector

A few minutes later, the continuous scan ran and the AMI showed Scanned in the Inspector console.

Package updates: the fix list

The most practical part of this page is Package updates. Instead of hundreds of CVEs, you get a list of packages with the installed version, the fixed version, how many findings each one clears and the worst severity. That’s the to-do list for the next image build.

The first time I opened it, the list showed 12 packages. A couple of minutes later it showed 72, so give it a few minutes and refresh before planning around it.

What I’d fix first:

  • kernel6.18 and kernel6.18-tools: 6.18.54 to 6.18.56, 20 findings each.
  • openssh, openssh-clients and openssh-server: 18 findings each.
  • org.jenkins-ci.plugins:git-client: 4.6.0 to 6.6.1. A Jenkins plugin in the same list as the OS packages.
  • runc: only Medium, but Exploit available: Yes. On a Jenkins box running Docker builds, I’d patch this before some of the Highs.

That last one is why I sort by Exploit available before severity. A Medium with public exploit code is often the more realistic risk.

The same CVE in Inspector findings

In Findings, filtering on the package name brings up CVE-2026-42523 against the AMI. The detail panel adds the CVSS vector, scores from both GitLab and NVD (9 from each), and the related advisory GHSA-w22p-4x9f-486v.

Export findings and Create suppression rule work for AMI findings like any other. The resource panel also says No resource tags, which confirms the “Excluded by tag” status earlier came from the copied-image setting.

// 12

Checking results from the CLI

On-demand results live on the AMI, so the CLI is the easy way to check an image in a pipeline before you promote it:

# Scan summary stored on the AMI
aws ec2 describe-images \
  --image-ids ami-0ae7035284bfe8f84 \
  --query "Images[].ScanResults"

# Detailed findings
aws ec2 get-image-findings --image-id ami-0ae7035284bfe8f84

get-image-findings is new, so check the EC2 CLI reference for the options your version supports.

// 13

What I’m doing next

This Jenkins AMI is going to be rebuilt with the kernel, OpenSSH and runc updates and newer plugins, then scanned again to compare.

For my own accounts, I’m keeping copied images included, setting the date rules to 60 days, and tagging throwaway lab AMIs so they’re skipped. Until now, an AMI was a black box until someone launched it. Now I can see what’s inside before it ever runs.
